item.title: Synthetic tools to redirect the ubiquitin E3 ligase activity of a plant-specific N-recognin
item.content:encoded:
Nature Communications, Published online: 30 October 2026; doi:10.1038/s41467-026-78958-z

The Arg/N-degron pathway plays a central role in plant development, germination, and submersion tolerance. Here, the authors show that PRT1 recruits the UBC35-UEV1A complex via RING1 of PRT1, demonstrate an off-switch for calmodulin-controlled ubiquitination, and engineer nanobodies that can redirect PRT1.

item.title: Weakened association between sequential phenological events corresponds to interphase extension
item.content:encoded:
Nature Communications, Published online: 30 October 2026; doi:10.1038/s41467-026-79161-w

Seasonal events in temperate deciduous trees, from leaf-out to leaf fall, follow a fixed annual sequence. This study shows that the timing of consecutive events is statistically associated in European trees, but that the association between fruiting and leaf coloration has weakened in some species as the interval between these phases has increased.
item.dc:title: Weakened association between sequential phenological events corresponds to interphase extension

item.title: Sequential protonation and deprotonation reactions govern alternating access in a Major Facilitator Superfamily proton/multidrug antiporter
item.content:encoded:
Nature Communications, Published online: 30 October 2026; doi:10.1038/s41467-026-78611-9

The molecular mechanisms underlying proton-coupled drug efflux are not fully resolved. Here the authors assess the timing and mechanism of proton coupling in the multidrug transporter LmrP, a prototypical exporter of clinically relevant antibiotics and toxins.

item.title: Process-dependent shifts in conspecific negative density dependence during boreal forest succession
item.content:encoded:
Nature Communications, Published online: 30 October 2026; doi:10.1038/s41467-026-79050-2

Conspecific negative density dependence may maintain diversity, but its role during succession is unclear. This study shows that changes depend on demographic processes and species abundance rather than following a uniform community-wide trend.

item.content:encoded:
Nature Communications, Published online: 30 October 2026; doi:10.1038/s41467-026-78965-0

Animals living in the deep sea often form symbiotic partnerships with chemosynthetic bacteria. Here authors discover a multilamellar organelle in the worm-mollusc Chaetoderma shenloong containing bacteria and name it dracosphera (‘dragon ball’).
